# Katsu-Hybrid-AIGC-Detector
Katsu is a lightweight, self-supervised-backbone hybrid model for detecting AI-generated images, built specifically to stay accurate after the image has been through real-world redistribution (recompression, resizing, cropping, noise). It combines a **frozen DINOv2-S/14 backbone** with two complementary, lightweight artifact-detection branches: an **NPR (upsampling-residual) branch** and a **texture-statistics (LBP/GLCM) branch**, fused through an **importance-weighted gating head**. Only **33,842 trainable parameters** sit on top of the frozen backbone. This model is built for Tik Tok's annual hackathon **TechJam 2026**.

      <p>Platforms already auto-label AI content via C2PA credentials and invisible watermarks —

      Once it's gone, there's nothing left to check.</p>

      confidence score instead of a binary label.</p>
    </div>

  <!-- ARCHITECTURE -->
  <div class="pill-row"><div class="pill">Model Architecture</div></div>
  <div class="row2">
    <div class="card acc-amber">
      <h3>Design Notes</h3>
      <ul>
        <li><b>DINOv2</b> is a vision model that learns what an image looks like just by studying pictures, without needing captions or labels. We use it because it was trained to recognize the same image even after it's been cropped or altered, which is exactly the kind of resilience we need.</li>
        <li><b>The NPR branch</b> looks at the tiny mismatches left behind when an image has been resized or upscaled at some point. We added it because AI generators tend to leave this kind of subtle resizing fingerprint, even when the image looks clean to the eye.</li>
        <li><b>The texture branch</b> measures patterns in how pixels sit next to each other, similar to how a forensic tool reads surface grain. We included it because it's a completely different kind of signal from the other two, so it catches cases they might miss.</li>
        <li><b>The fusion step</b> decides, for each image, how much to trust each of the three signals above instead of averaging them blindly. We use it because different images get caught by different signals, so a fixed formula would underperform an adaptive one.</li>
      </ul>
      <div class="stat-row">

          <div class="branch npr">Upsample ↓↑<br><span style="font-weight:400;">then subtract from original</span></div>
          <div class="branch tex">LBP + GLCM<br><span style="font-weight:400;">texture statistics</span></div>
        </div>
        <div class="flow-arrow" style="margin-top:-4px;">↓</div>
        <div class="branch-grid">
          <div class="branch frozen" style="opacity:0.85;">384-d CLS<br>embedding</div>
          <div class="branch npr" style="opacity:0.85;">Shallow CNN<br>→ 32-d embedding</div>
          <div class="branch tex" style="opacity:0.85;">Linear proj.<br>→ 32-d embedding</div>
        </div>

        <div class="converge"></div>
        <div class="flow-box fuse">Gating network: learns how much to trust each branch, per image</div>
        <div class="flow-arrow">↓</div>
        <div class="flow-box" style="background:#c4b5fd0d; border:1px dashed var(--text-dim); color:var(--text); font-weight:400;">weighted sum → fused 64-d representation</div>
        <div class="flow-arrow">↓</div>
        <div class="flow-box" style="background:#e8edf9;">Classifier head (Linear → ReLU → Linear)</div>
        <div class="flow-arrow">↓</div>
        <div class="flow-box out">Confidence Score (0–1, likelihood AI-generated)</div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

      <tr><td>F1</td><td style="color:var(--amber); font-weight:600;">0.813</td><td style="color:var(--cyan); font-weight:600;">0.848</td></tr>

      <tr><td>False negative rate</td><td style="color:var(--amber); font-weight:600;">0.203</td><td style="color:var(--cyan); font-weight:600;">0.220</td></tr>
    </table>
    <p style="font-size:11px; color:var(--text-dim); margin-top:8px; margin-bottom:0;">
      *Reserved benchmark = COCO val2017 (real) + DALL&middot;E 3 Advanced (fake), organizer-mandated, eval-only.
    </p>

    <div class="callout">
      <b>Key observation:</b> the model scores slightly higher on the reserved, organizer-mandated

  <!-- DATASETS -->

      <tr><td>WildFake — COCO val2017 + DALL·E 3 Advanced</td><td><span class="tag tag-reserved">RESERVED BENCHMARK</span> eval-only</td><td>4,998 real + 8,843 fake</td></tr>
    </table>

  <!-- TECH STACK -->

## How This Solution Addresses the Problem Statement

Platforms like TikTok already auto-label AI-generated content via C2PA Content Credentials and invisible watermarks, but that provenance metadata is stripped the moment content is screenshotted, re-encoded, or reposted off-platform. Once that happens, there's no metadata left to check.

Katsu is a **content-based fallback layer** for exactly that scenario: it doesn't rely on any embedded signal, only the pixels themselves, and it's trained specifically to keep working after the kinds of transformations that strip metadata in the first place. That's the "redistribution robustness" this problem statement is testing — not just detecting AI-generated images in their original, clean form.
